lessons.title: Rotating field, slip and rotor quantities

scenes.text: Over two-thirds of industrial electrical energy drives induction motors.
A rotating field 'drags' the rotor along — it can never quite catch up.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
N_s = 120f/P. Slip s = (N_s − N)/N_s. Rotor frequency f_r = sf. Rotor EMF E₂ₛ = sE₂ (E₂ at standstill). Rotor reactance X₂ₛ = sX₂. Rotor current I₂ = sE₂/√(R₂² + (sX₂)²).
A three-phase winding fed with balanced currents produces a constant-magnitude field (1.5 × Φ_max per phase) rotating at N_s.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 6-pole, 50 Hz at 960 rpm: N_s = 1000, s = 0.04, f_r = 2 Hz.

**Example 2.** Rotor standstill EMF 100 V/phase, R₂ = 0.05 Ω, X₂ = 0.5 Ω, s = 0.04: E₂ₛ = 4 V, X₂ₛ = 0.02 Ω ⇒ I₂ = 4/√(0.0025 + 0.0004) = 74.3 A.

**Example 3.** Reversing two supply leads reverses the field and the motor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rotor speed instead of N_s in f_r.
- Forgetting reactance scales with s.
- Thinking the motor can run at s = 0 under load.

activity.prompt: 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor at 1455 rpm. Slip in percent?

quiz.why: Rotor frequency f_r = sf = 0.05 × 50 = 2.5 Hz. The slip tells how fast the rotor lags the field.
Rotor EMF is proportional to the relative speed between the field and the rotor, so at slip s it is sE₂, where E₂ is the EMF at standstill.
Swapping any two of the three supply phases reverses the direction of the rotating field, and so the motor reverses.
Induction motors run with a small slip at full load, typically 2–6%. A slip of 0 would give no torque.

scenes.text: A 15 kW motor draws 17 kW — the difference is lost as heat and friction.
The equivalent circuit splits rotor input into copper loss and mechanical power.

steps.title: Power flow
steps.body:
Input → stator Cu and core loss → air-gap power P_ag (rotor input).
Rotor Cu loss = sP_ag; gross mechanical power P_m = (1 − s)P_ag; P_ag : P_cu2 : P_m = 1 : s : (1 − s).
Shaft output = P_m − friction & windage. Torque T = P_ag/ω_s = P_m/ω_r.
Equivalent circuit (per phase, referred to stator): R₁ + jX₁, magnetising branch, then jX₂′ and R₂′/s = R₂′ + R₂′(1 − s)/s (load resistance).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** P_ag = 20 kW at s = 0.04: rotor Cu = 800 W; P_m = 19.2 kW. Torque at 1500 rpm sync: T = 20 000/157.08 = 127.3 N·m.

**Example 2.** Motor input 50 kW, stator losses 2 kW, s = 0.03, friction 1 kW: P_ag = 48 kW; rotor Cu = 1.44 kW; P_m = 46.56 kW; output 45.56 kW; η = 91.1%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing torque with rotor speed from air-gap power (use ω_s with P_ag).
- Forgetting that rotor copper loss = s × air-gap power.
- Missing mechanical losses in output.

activity.prompt: Power flow of an induction motor
items: Electrical input to stator
Subtract stator copper and core losses ⇒ air-gap power
Subtract rotor copper loss (s × P_ag) ⇒ gross mechanical power
Subtract friction and windage ⇒ shaft output

quiz.why: Air-gap power splits as rotor copper loss = sP_ag and mechanical power = (1 − s)P_ag. So rotor copper loss = s × P_ag.
Gross mechanical power is the part of air-gap power that is not lost in the rotor: P_m = (1 − s)P_ag.
The torque is T = P_ag/ω_s, where ω_s is the synchronous angular speed. The air-gap power is transferred at synchronous speed.
In the equivalent circuit, the mechanical power is shown as power in a load resistor R₂′(1 − s)/s, since R₂′/s = R₂′ + R₂′(1 − s)/s.
At standstill s = 1, so (1 − s) = 0 and the mechanical power is zero, though there is torque. All air-gap power is lost as rotor heat.

scenes.text: A crusher motor stalls if the load exceeds its pull-out torque.
The torque–slip curve shows starting, maximum and full-load torques.

steps.title: Torque expressions
steps.body:
T = (3/ω_s) × V²(R₂′/s)/[(R₁ + R₂′/s)² + (X₁ + X₂′)²] (per-phase V).
Neglecting stator impedance: T ∝ sR₂/(R₂² + s²X₂²).
Maximum torque at s_m = R₂/X₂ (independent of R₂ in magnitude): T_max ∝ E₂²/(2X₂).
Low slip region: T ∝ s (linear, stable); high slip: T ∝ 1/s.
T/T_max = 2s s_m/(s² + s_m²). Starting torque maximum when R₂ = X₂.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** R₂ = 0.02 Ω, X₂ = 0.1 Ω: s_m = 0.2 ⇒ at N_s = 1500, speed at max torque = 1200 rpm.

**Example 2.** T_st/T_max = 2(1)(0.2)/(1 + 0.04) = 0.385.

**Example 3.** Full-load slip 0.04: T_FL/T_max = 2(0.04)(0.2)/(0.0016 + 0.04) = 0.385. To get T_st = T_max, add external rotor resistance so R₂ = X₂ = 0.1 Ω (slip-ring motor).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking adding rotor resistance changes T_max (it changes only where it occurs).
- Using line voltage in per-phase torque formula.
- Forgetting T ∝ V² (a 10% voltage dip reduces torque by ~19%).

activity.label: Slip (as fraction) for a motor with s_m = 0.2

bands.text: Low slip: torque rises almost linearly — stable running region.
High slip up to standstill (s = 1): torque falls; s = 1 gives starting torque.

quiz.why: Maximum torque occurs at slip s_m = R₂/X₂, where the rotor resistance equals the standstill rotor reactance.
Adding rotor resistance moves the slip of maximum torque to a higher value (s_m = R₂/X₂), but T_max itself is unchanged. This also improves starting torque.

quiz.q: Torque varies with supply voltage as
quiz.why: Torque is proportional to the square of the supply voltage, T ∝ V², since the rotor EMF and the current are both proportional to V.
Starting torque is maximum when s_m = 1, i.e. R₂ = X₂. Then the maximum torque of the motor occurs right at standstill.
The stable region is where torque rises with slip, from 0 up to s_m, so a small slowdown raises torque and restores the speed. Beyond s_m, the slope is negative and the motor stalls.

lessons.title: Starting, speed control, induction generator and single-phase motors

scenes.text: A 30 kW borewell pump motor would draw 6–7× rated current direct-on-line.
A star–delta starter cuts starting current to one third.

steps.title: Starting methods
steps.body:
- DOL: I_st ≈ 5–7 I_FL; small motors.
- Star–delta: starting phase voltage 1/√3 ⇒ line current and torque 1/3 of DOL.
- Autotransformer (tap x): current and torque × x².
- Rotor resistance (slip-ring): high torque, low current.
- Soft starters/VFDs: smooth, controllable.

steps.title: Speed control and others
steps.body:
Speed control: V/f control with VFDs (constant flux, most common today), pole changing, rotor resistance (slip-ring), slip-power recovery.
**Induction generator:** driven above N_s (negative slip); needs reactive power (grid or capacitors) — wind turbines.
**Single-phase induction motors:** pulsating field = two counter-rotating fields (double revolving field theory) ⇒ no starting torque; use split-phase, capacitor-start, capacitor-run, shaded-pole designs (fans, pumps, compressors).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** DOL starting current 6 I_FL, T_st = 1.8 T_FL ⇒ star–delta: 2 I_FL and 0.6 T_FL.

**Example 2.** Autotransformer 70% tap: current from line = 0.49 × 6 = 2.94 I_FL; torque 0.88 T_FL.

**Example 3.** V/f: 400 V 50 Hz motor run at 25 Hz ⇒ apply ~200 V to keep flux constant.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Star–delta on a motor not designed for delta running.
- Reducing frequency without reducing voltage (saturation, overheating).
- Thinking a single-phase motor self-starts without auxiliary winding.

activity.prompt: Starter → starting current (relative to DOL)

quiz.why: In star, the phase voltage is 1/√3 of the delta value, so torque (∝ V²) falls to 1/3 of that for direct-on-line (DOL) starting. Line current also falls to 1/3.
Most modern drives use variable-frequency drives (VFDs) with V/f control, since they are efficient and give smooth control over a wide range of speeds.
If the rotor is driven above synchronous speed, the slip becomes negative and the machine delivers power to the supply, i.e. it acts as an induction generator.

quiz.q: Single-phase IM has no starting torque because
quiz.why: A single-phase winding produces a pulsating field, which can be seen as two equal fields rotating in opposite directions. They cancel at standstill, so there is no starting torque.
Ceiling fans use single-phase capacitor-run motors. The capacitor produces a phase-shifted auxiliary winding current, giving a rotating field and starting torque.

questions.q: Synchronous speed formula
questions.why: N_s = 120f/P, where f is the frequency in Hz and P the number of poles. For example, 120 × 50/4 = 1500 rpm.

questions.q: Squirrel-cage rotor bars are
questions.why: In a squirrel-cage rotor, the bars are permanently short-circuited at both ends by end rings, so there are no slip rings or external connections.
options: insulated from each other at ends

questions.q: Induction motor speed is
questions.why: The rotor must run slower than the field to cut the flux and have an induced current. So the speed is slightly less than synchronous speed.

questions.q: Rotor Cu loss at s = 0.05, P_ag = 10 kW
questions.why: Rotor copper loss = sP_ag = 0.05 × 10 kW = 0.5 kW = 500 W. The rest, 9.5 kW, is the mechanical power.

questions.q: Speed of 4-pole 50 Hz motor at 4% slip
Star–delta starter line current relative to DOL
questions.why: In star, the phase voltage is reduced by 1/√3, so the phase current also falls by 1/√3. Since line current in delta is √3 × phase current, the line current drops to 1/3 of the DOL value.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Maximum torque of an induction motor is independent of rotor resistance.  Reason (R): Rotor resistance only shifts the slip at which maximum torque occurs.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. T_max depends on the rotor reactance and the voltage (T_max ∝ E²/2X₂), not on R₂. Changing R₂ only shifts the slip at which T_max occurs (s_m = R₂/X₂), so R explains A.

questions.q: s_m for R₂ = 0.04, X₂ = 0.2 Ω
questions.why: s_m = R₂/X₂ = 0.04/0.2 = 0.2. The maximum torque occurs at 20% slip.

questions.q: Torque if voltage falls to 90%
questions.why: Torque ∝ V², so at 90% voltage the torque is 0.9² = 0.81 of its normal value, i.e. 81%. A small voltage drop causes a bigger torque drop.

questions.q: T at P_ag = 30 kW, N_s = 1000 rpm
Case: A 22 kW pump motor on a weak supply trips on DOL start. Cheapest effective fix for a delta-rated motor
questions.why: A star–delta starter reduces the starting current to 1/3 of DOL and is cheap, but needs a motor rated for delta running. So it is the cheapest effective fix. A larger fuse or bigger motor would not reduce the supply dip.

questions.q: T_st/T_max for s_m = 0.25
questions.why: T/T_max = 2s s_m/(s² + s_m²); at starting s = 1 this gives 2s_m/(1 + s_m²) = 0.5/1.0625 ≈ 0.47.

questions.q: Input 40 kW, stator loss 1.5 kW, s = 0.04, F&W 0.6 kW: output
questions.why: P_ag = 40 − 1.5 = 38.5 kW. P_m = (1 − 0.04) × 38.5 = 36.96 kW. Output = 36.96 − 0.6 = 36.36 ≈ 36.4 kW after friction and windage.

questions.q: External rotor resistance per phase to get T_st = T_max with R₂ = 0.05, X₂ = 0.4
questions.why: Starting torque is maximum when s_m = 1, i.e. total rotor resistance = X₂ = 0.4 Ω. So R_ext = 0.4 − 0.05 = 0.35 Ω per phase.

questions.q: Autotransformer starter tap for starting current 2× FL when DOL is 6× FL
questions.why: Starting current ∝ x² times DOL current (x = tap fraction). We want 2/6 = 1/3, so x² = 1/3 and x = 0.577, i.e. about 57.7% tap.

scenes.text: A 500 MW turbo-alternator spins at 3000 rpm with a 2-pole cylindrical rotor.
Hydro alternators turn slowly with many salient poles.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body: Stationary armature (stator) and rotating DC field (rotor) via slip rings or brushless exciter. Cylindrical (non-salient) rotors: high speed (steam/gas turbines, 2 or 4 poles). Salient poles: low speed (hydro, diesel), many poles. N_s = 120f/P.

steps.title: EMF equation and winding factors
steps.body:
E_ph = 4.44 f Φ T_ph K_p K_d (T_ph = turns per phase).
Pitch (coil-span) factor K_p = cos(α/2), α = chording angle (electrical).
Distribution factor K_d = sin(mβ/2)/(m sin(β/2)), m = slots per pole per phase, β = slot angle (electrical) = 180°P/S (S slots).
Short pitching (e.g. 5/6) reduces harmonics (5th, 7th).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 3-phase, 4-pole, 36 slots: m = 3, β = 20°. K_d = sin 30°/(3 sin 10°) = 0.5/0.521 = 0.960. Coil span 8 slots (full pitch 9) ⇒ α = 20° ⇒ K_p = cos 10° = 0.985.

**Example 2.** f = 50 Hz, Φ = 0.05 Wb, T_ph = 120: E = 4.44 × 50 × 0.05 × 120 × 0.985 × 0.960 = 1260 V/phase (≈ 2182 V line in star).

**Example 3.** Hydro alternator 50 Hz at 150 rpm ⇒ P = 40 poles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using mechanical instead of electrical angles in K_d and K_p.
- Forgetting that line voltage = √3 × phase in star.
- Counting conductors instead of turns.

activity.prompt: 50 Hz alternator at 300 rpm. Number of poles?

quiz.why: Turbo-alternators run at high speed (1500–3000 rpm) with few poles, and their long, slim rotors are cylindrical (non-salient) for mechanical strength.
Pitch factor K_p = cos(α/2), where α is the angle by which the coil is short of full pitch (in electrical degrees). For full pitch α = 0 and K_p = 1.
The slot angle in electrical degrees is β = 180° × P/slots. Here: 180 × 4/48 = 15°.
Short-pitch coils cut out some harmonics (such as the 3rd, 5th, 7th) from the EMF waveform, with only a small loss of the fundamental.

quiz.q: Field winding of an alternator is on
quiz.why: In most alternators, the DC field winding is on the rotor, fed through slip rings, and the AC armature winding is on the stator. This avoids taking high power through slip rings.

lessons.title: Armature reaction, synchronous reactance and regulation

scenes.text: An isolated diesel generator's voltage drops when a large motor starts.
Synchronous reactance models armature reaction plus leakage.

steps.title: Armature reaction by pf
steps.body:
Unity pf: cross-magnetising. Zero lagging: demagnetising (needs more field). Zero leading: magnetising. Synchronous reactance X_s = X_l + X_ar; Z_s = R_a + jX_s.
Per phase: E = V + I(R_a + jX_s).

steps.title: Regulation (EMF / synchronous impedance method)
steps.body:
Z_s from OC and SC tests at the same field current: Z_s = E_oc/I_sc. Regulation = (E − V)/V × 100. Pessimistic method (overestimates) because it assumes linear magnetics; MMF (optimistic) and ZPF/Potier (accurate) methods also used.
Lagging pf ⇒ positive regulation; leading pf may give negative regulation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using line voltage in per-phase equations.
- Sign of the current angle for leading vs lagging.
- Taking Z_s from OC and SC values at different field currents.

activity.prompt: OC voltage 500 V/phase and SC current 100 A at the same field current. Z_s (Ω)?

quiz.why: At zero-pf lagging load, the armature current lags the EMF by 90°, and its flux directly opposes the main field. This is demagnetising armature reaction.
Synchronous impedance is Z_s = E_oc/I_sc, taken at the same field current in the open- and short-circuit tests.
The EMF method ignores saturation and treats Z_s as constant. It overestimates the voltage rise needed, so it gives a higher regulation, i.e. a pessimistic result.
At a leading power factor, armature reaction is magnetising, and the terminal voltage can exceed the no-load EMF, making regulation negative.
The synchronous reactance X_s is the sum of the leakage reactance and the reactance that represents armature reaction. R_a is separate.

scenes.text: Before closing the breaker, operators watch a synchroscope.
Closing out of phase can damage the machine with huge currents.

steps.title: Synchronising conditions
steps.body:
Equal voltage, equal frequency, same phase sequence, and zero phase angle at closing. Methods: lamps (dark/bright lamp), synchroscope, automatic synchronisers.
Once on an infinite bus: real power controlled by prime-mover input (governor); reactive power and pf controlled by field excitation.

steps.title: Power–angle relation
steps.body:
Cylindrical rotor (R_a neglected): P = (3EV/X_s) sin δ (three-phase, per-phase E, V). Maximum (steady-state limit) at δ = 90°: P_max = 3EV/X_s. Salient pole adds a reluctance term (V²/2)(1/X_q − 1/X_d) sin 2δ.
Synchronising power coefficient P_s = dP/dδ = (3EV/X_s) cos δ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** E = 1.2 pu, V = 1.0 pu, X_s = 1.0 pu, P = 0.6 pu: sin δ = 0.5 ⇒ δ = 30°. P_max = 1.2 pu.

**Example 2.** Increasing excitation with the same P: E rises ⇒ δ falls; machine supplies more lagging reactive power (over-excited).

**Example 3.** Per-phase E = 2500 V, V = 2400 V, X_s = 10 Ω, δ = 20°: P = 3 × 2500 × 2400 × 0.342/10 = 615.6 kW.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking excitation changes real power (governor does).
- Using single-phase formula for three-phase power.
- Operating near δ = 90° (no margin — loss of synchronism).

activity.prompt: Synchronising an alternator to the bus
items: Bring the machine to near-synchronous speed with the prime mover
Adjust excitation so terminal voltage equals bus voltage
Check phase sequence matches
Adjust speed until the synchroscope pointer turns very slowly
Close the breaker at the in-phase position

quiz.q: Real power output is controlled by
quiz.why: For a grid-connected alternator, real power is set by the mechanical power from the prime mover (governor). Excitation only affects the reactive power.
Reactive power output is controlled by the field excitation. Over-excitation makes the alternator supply lagging VARs, under-excitation makes it absorb.
Power P = (EV/X)sinδ is maximum at δ = 90°. Beyond that, a larger δ gives less power, so the machine goes unstable. That is the steady-state limit.

quiz.q: P for E = V = 1 pu, X = 0.5 pu, δ = 30°

quiz.why: Synchronising needs equal voltage, frequency and phase sequence (and phase angle). The two machines can have different kVA ratings.

scenes.text: A cement plant runs a large over-excited synchronous motor on its mill.
It drives the load AND supplies reactive power, improving the plant's pf.

steps.title: Operation
steps.body:
Runs only at N_s; not self-starting (rotor can't follow the field from rest). Starting: damper (amortisseur) windings as induction motor, pony motor, or VFD.
V-curves: armature current vs field current at constant load — minimum at unity pf; under-excited ⇒ lagging pf, over-excited ⇒ leading pf. Inverted-V curves: pf vs field current.
Synchronous condenser: over-excited motor at no load — variable reactive power source.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Plant: 800 kW at 0.7 lag (Q = 816 kVAR). Add a 300 kW synchronous motor at 0.8 lead (Q = −225 kVAR): total P = 1100 kW, Q = 591 kVAR ⇒ pf = 0.88 lag.

**Example 2.** To reach unity overall, the motor must supply 816 kVAR ⇒ its kVA = √(300² + 816²) = 869 kVA.

**Example 3.** 6-pole 50 Hz synchronous motor speed = 1000 rpm at any load (within pull-out).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting slip in a synchronous motor.
- Confusing under-excited (lagging) with over-excited (leading).
- Forgetting damper windings also damp hunting.

activity.prompt: Excitation state of a synchronous motor

items.text: Minimum armature current for given load
Supplies reactive power to the system

quiz.why: A synchronous motor locks to the rotating field, so its speed is exactly the synchronous speed N_s at any load, as long as it stays in synchronism.

quiz.q: Bottom of a V-curve corresponds to
quiz.why: On a V-curve (armature current vs field current), the lowest current is at unity power factor. Either side, the current rises with a lagging or leading pf.
A synchronous condenser is a synchronous motor run at no load, with over-excitation, so that it supplies reactive power to the grid like a capacitor.
options: an over-excited motor at no load

quiz.why: A synchronous motor has no starting torque by itself. It is started with damper (amortisseur) windings, as an induction motor, or by a VFD, and then synchronised.
An over-excited synchronous motor draws a leading current, i.e. it supplies reactive power, so its power factor is leading.

questions.q: Hydro alternators typically have
questions.why: Hydro turbines run slowly, so the alternators need many poles to give 50 Hz. These have large-diameter rotors with salient poles.

questions.q: EMF equation constant
questions.why: The EMF equation for an alternator is E = 4.44 f Φ T K_p K_d, the same form as the transformer EMF equation.

questions.q: Synchronous motors are self-starting?
questions.why: Synchronous motors have no starting torque, since the rotor cannot lock on to a fast-rotating field from rest. They need damper windings or a drive.

questions.q: Speed of 4-pole 60 Hz alternator
Pitch factor for 150° coil span
questions.why: A 150° span is 30° short of full pitch (180°), so α = 30° and K_p = cos(α/2) = cos 15° ≈ 0.966.

questions.q: Regulation if E = 260 V, V = 230 V
Assertion (A): Increasing excitation of a grid-connected alternator mainly changes reactive power.  Reason (R): Real power is set by the prime mover; excitation changes E and the reactive output.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Real power is fixed by the prime mover, so excitation changes E and the reactive power only. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: K_d for m = 2, β = 30°
E for V = 1 pu, I = 1 pu at unity pf, X_s = 0.8 pu
questions.why: At unity pf, E = √(V² + (IX_s)²) = √(1 + 0.64) ≈ 1.28 pu. The IX_s drop is at 90° to V, so it adds in quadrature.

questions.q: δ for P = 0.8 pu, E = 1.6, V = 1, X_s = 1
questions.why: P = (EV/X_s)sinδ gives 0.8 = 1.6 × 1/1 × sinδ, so sinδ = 0.5 and δ = 30°.

questions.q: Case: A plant runs 600 kW at 0.6 lag. A synchronous motor taking 200 kW is added to make the overall pf 1. Motor kVAR (leading)
questions.why: At 0.6 pf, the plant has P = 600 kW and Q = 600 × tan(53.13°) = 800 kVAR lagging. For unity pf overall, the motor must supply 800 kVAR leading.

questions.q: Motor kVA for that case
questions.why: The motor kVA = √(P² + Q²) = √(200² + 800²) = √680000 ≈ 825 kVA. The kVA is bigger than the real power because of the large reactive part.

questions.q: Regulation with V = 1, I = 1 pu at 0.8 lag, X_s = 1 pu, R = 0
Synchronising power coefficient at δ = 30° (P_max = 1.2 pu)
questions.why: The synchronising power coefficient is dP/dδ = P_max cosδ = 1.2 × cos 30° = 1.2 × 0.866 ≈ 1.04 pu per rad. It measures the restoring effect.

questions.q: Distribution factor for 3-phase, 6-pole, 54 slots
questions.why: Slots per pole per phase m = 54/(6 × 3) = 3. Slot angle β = 180 × 6/54 = 20°. K_d = sin(60°/... ) = sin(mβ/2)/(m sin(β/2)) = sin 30°/(3 sin 10°) = 0.5/0.521 ≈ 0.960.

steps.title: Transformers
steps.body:

quiz.why: The short-circuit test is done at rated current, so the input power is almost entirely copper loss. The iron loss is negligible because the voltage is low.
A wave winding always has 2 parallel paths, independent of the number of poles.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Rotor Cu loss 5% slip, P_ag 20 kW
quiz.why: Rotor copper loss = sP_ag = 0.05 × 20 kW = 1 kW.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Alternator real power is set by
quiz.why: Real power from an alternator on the grid is controlled by the mechanical input from the prime mover (governor). Excitation controls reactive power.
An under-excited synchronous motor draws a lagging current, like an inductor, so its pf is lagging. Over-excitation gives leading pf.
A star–delta starter applies the reduced voltage in star, so the line current is 1/3 of the direct-on-line current.

questions.q: Core of a transformer is laminated to reduce
questions.why: The core is made from thin insulated laminations to break the paths of eddy currents. This reduces eddy-current loss, a part of iron loss.

questions.q: DC motor for traction
questions.why: A DC series motor gives very high torque at low speed (T ∝ I_a²), which suits traction loads like trains and trams.

questions.q: N_s for 2-pole 50 Hz
Synchronous condenser supplies
questions.why: An over-excited synchronous machine running at no load supplies reactive power to the grid, which helps with voltage control and power factor.

questions.q: η of 25 kVA transformer at FL, pf 0.8, P_i 250 W, P_cu 500 W
Rotor EMF at s = 0.03 if standstill E₂ = 120 V
questions.why: Rotor EMF = sE₂ = 0.03 × 120 = 3.6 V. At low slip the rotor EMF is small.

questions.q: Shunt motor speed if Φ reduced 10% (E_b ~ const)
questions.why: N ∝ E_b/Φ. If Φ falls by 10% and E_b stays about the same, N becomes 1/0.9 ≈ 1.11 times. Weaker field means higher speed.

questions.q: Torque at P_ag 15 kW, 1500 rpm sync
Assertion (A): A DC series motor's speed rises sharply at light load.  Reason (R): Flux falls with armature current and N ∝ E_b/Φ.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. In a series motor, the flux falls as armature current falls, and N ∝ E_b/Φ, so at light load the speed rises sharply. R explains A.

questions.q: Autotransformer 240/200 V, 12 kVA: transformed kVA
questions.why: The power transformed (by induction) in an autotransformer is S(1 − V_low/V_high) = 12 × (1 − 200/240) = 12 × 0.1667 = 2 kVA. The rest is conducted directly.

questions.q: E per phase: f 50, Φ 0.04, T 100, K_p 0.96, K_d 0.96
T_FL/T_max for s = 0.05, s_m = 0.25
Case: Two transformers 600 kVA (4%) and 400 kVA (6%) share 900 kVA. 400 kVA unit carries
Regulation: V 1 pu, I 1 pu unity pf, R 0.05, X_s 1.2 pu
Swinburne: 250 V, no-load 5 A, I_sh 1 A, R_a 0.2 Ω — constant losses
questions.why: Input at no load = 250 × 5 = 1250 W. Armature copper loss = (5 − 1)² × 0.2 = 3.2 W. Constant losses = 1250 − 3.2 = 1246.8 W.

questions.q: Speed of a 4-pole induction motor whose rotor current frequency is 1.5 Hz on 50 Hz
questions.why: Rotor current frequency = sf, so s = 1.5/50 = 0.03. N_s = 1500 rpm, so N = 1500 × 0.97 = 1455 rpm.

questions.q: Starting torque with autotransformer at 60% tap if DOL T_st = 2 T_FL
questions.why: Starting torque scales with the square of the tap fraction: 0.6² = 0.36. So T_st = 0.36 × 2 T_FL = 0.72 T_FL.

questions.q: Power at δ = 25°: E 11 kV line, V 11 kV line, X_s 8 Ω per phase (3-phase)
questions.why: Phase voltage = 11 kV/√3. 3-phase power = V_L E_L sinδ/X_s = (11000 × 11000 × sin 25°)/8 = 121×10⁶ × 0.4226/8 ≈ 6.39 MW.

questions.q: Pull-out torque ratio if supply voltage falls 20%
questions.why: Pull-out (maximum) torque is proportional to V². At 80% voltage, the ratio is 0.8² = 0.64.

lessons.title: Power system structure and load characteristics

scenes.text: Power demand at 3 a.m. is much lower than at 7 p.m.
Utilities plan plants using load curves, load factor and diversity factor.

steps.title: Structure and generation
steps.body: Generation (thermal, hydro, nuclear, gas, solar, wind) → step-up → transmission (e.g. 220/400/765 kV AC, HVDC) → sub-transmission → distribution (33/11 kV, 415/230 V). Base-load plants (nuclear, coal) run continuously; peak-load (gas, hydro, storage) follow demand. Renewables are variable — storage and forecasting help.

steps.title: Load factors
steps.body:
- Load factor = average load/maximum demand.
- Demand factor = maximum demand/connected load.
- Diversity factor = Σ individual max demands/system max demand (≥ 1).
- Plant capacity factor = average load/plant capacity.
- Plant use factor = actual energy/(capacity × hours used).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Max demand 50 MW, annual energy 262.8 GWh ⇒ average = 262.8×10⁶ kWh/8760 h = 30 MW ⇒ load factor = 30/50 = 0.6.

**Example 2.** Three consumers with max demands 10, 15, 20 kW; combined max 30 kW ⇒ diversity factor 1.5.

**Example 3.** Plant 60 MW, average load 30 MW ⇒ capacity factor 0.5.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Diversity factor less than 1 (impossible).
- Mixing kWh and kW.
- Using connected load instead of maximum demand in load factor.

activity.prompt: Max demand 80 MW, annual energy 420.48 GWh. Load factor (decimal)?

quiz.why: Load factor = average load/maximum demand. It is a measure of how steadily a plant is used over the period.
Diversity factor = (sum of individual maximum demands)/(maximum demand of the whole system). Since individual peaks do not coincide, it is always ≥ 1.
Base-load plants (nuclear, large coal) run steadily at high output as they are costly to start and have low running cost. Peakers like gas or diesel serve short peaks.
A high load factor spreads fixed costs over more kWh sold, so cost per kWh falls and equipment is better used.
Low-voltage three-phase distribution in India is 415 V line-to-line (240 V per phase). 11 kV and 33 kV are primary distribution voltages.

scenes.text: A grid with dozens of transformers is analysed in per-unit.
Transformers disappear (become 1:1) and numbers become comparable.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Per-unit = actual/base. Choose S_base (3-phase MVA) and V_base (line kV) in one zone; V_base changes by transformer ratios across zones.
Z_base = V_base²/S_base (kV²/MVA = Ω); I_base = S_base/(√3 V_base).
Change of base: Z_new = Z_old × (V_old/V_new)² × (S_new/S_old).
Per-unit impedance of a transformer is the same referred to either side.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 132 kV, 100 MVA base: Z_base = 132²/100 = 174.2 Ω; a 50 Ω line = 0.287 pu.

**Example 2.** Generator 50 MVA, 11 kV, X = 0.2 pu → on 100 MVA, 11 kV base: 0.2 × 100/50 = 0.4 pu.

**Example 3.** Motor 0.15 pu on 10 MVA, 6.6 kV → base 100 MVA, 6.9 kV: 0.15 × (6.6/6.9)² × 10 = 1.372 pu.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using phase voltage with three-phase MVA in Z_base.
- Forgetting to change V_base across transformers.
- Changing base with S ratio inverted.

activity.prompt: Z_base for 33 kV and 100 MVA base (Ω)?

quiz.why: Base impedance Z_base = V_base²/S_base. With V in kV and S in MVA, Z_base is in ohms.

quiz.q: Transformer per-unit impedance referred to either side
quiz.why: The per-unit impedance of a transformer is the same on either side, since the bases transform with the turns ratio. That is a big advantage of the per-unit system.
To change base, pu Z_new = pu Z_old × (S_new/S_old) at the same voltage: 0.1 × 100/20 = 0.5 pu.
In the per-unit system, the normal voltage is about 1.0 pu, because values are divided by their nominal base. A normal bus voltage varies about ±5%.

scenes.text: Towers space conductors metres apart and often use bundles of 2–4 sub-conductors.
Spacing and bundling set the line inductance.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Single-phase two-wire: L = 4×10⁻⁷ ln(D/r′) H/m per loop (2×10⁻⁷ per conductor), r′ = 0.7788r (GMR of solid round conductor).
Three-phase (transposed): L = 2×10⁻⁷ ln(GMD/GMR) H/m per phase, GMD = ∛(D_ab D_bc D_ca).
Bundle GMR: 2 conductors √(r′d); 3 conductors ∛(r′d²); 4 conductors 1.09⁴√(r′d³).
Transposition balances inductances of the three phases.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Equilateral 3-phase, D = 2 m, r = 1 cm: r′ = 0.7788 cm; L = 2×10⁻⁷ ln(200/0.7788) = 2×10⁻⁷ × 5.548 = 1.11 mH/km.

**Example 2.** Flat spacing 4 m, 4 m, 8 m: GMD = ∛(4·4·8) = 5.04 m.

**Example 3.** Two-conductor bundle, r′ = 1.2 cm, d = 40 cm: GMR = √(1.2 × 40) = 6.93 cm — much larger ⇒ lower L, less corona.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using r instead of r′ for inductance (r is used for capacitance).
- Forgetting to convert to consistent units in ln(D/r).
- Per-loop vs per-conductor confusion in single-phase lines.

activity.prompt: 3-phase flat spacing 3 m, 3 m, 6 m. GMD (m, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: The GMR of a solid round conductor is r′ = e^(−1/4) r = 0.7788r, which accounts for flux inside the conductor.
Bundling several sub-conductors increases the effective GMR and effective radius. This lowers inductance and reduces the surface electric stress, so there is less corona.
For equilateral spacing, all three distances are D, so the GMD is D (the geometric mean of three equal numbers).
Transposing the conductors changes the positions of the phases along the line so each takes every position for one third of the length. This balances the phase inductances (and capacitances).
The inductance per phase is L = 2×10⁻⁷ ln(GMD/GMR) H/m. The GMD is the spacing and GMR the conductor's effective radius.

lessons.title: Capacitance, skin effect and the Ferranti effect

story.title: Rising voltage at a lightly loaded end

scenes.text: At night, the far end of a long cable can show higher voltage than the sending end.
Line capacitance causes the Ferranti effect.

steps.title: Capacitance
steps.body:
Three-phase transposed: C = 2πε₀/ln(GMD/r) F/m to neutral (uses actual radius r; bundle: GMR_C with r instead of r′).
Single-phase: C_ab = πε₀/ln(D/r). Charging current I_c = V_ph ωC per phase.
Earth effect slightly increases capacitance.

steps.title: Skin, proximity and Ferranti
steps.body:
**Skin effect:** AC current crowds towards the surface ⇒ higher effective resistance (worse at higher frequency/larger conductors) — ACSR stranding helps. **Proximity effect:** nearby conductors further distort current distribution.
**Ferranti effect:** under light load, capacitive charging current through series inductance makes receiving-end voltage exceed sending-end; V_R ≈ V_S/(1 − ω²LCl²/2) for long lines. Controlled by shunt reactors.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** D = 2 m, r = 1 cm: C = 2π × 8.854×10⁻¹²/ln(200) = 5.563×10⁻¹¹/5.298 = 10.5 nF/km.

**Example 2.** 220 kV, 100 km, C = 10 nF/km: I_c = (220 000/√3) × 314.16 × 10⁻⁶ = 39.9 A per phase.

**Example 3.** Ferranti rise for a 300 km line (βl ≈ 0.32 rad): V_R/V_S ≈ 1/cos(0.32) ≈ 1.053 (≈ 5% rise).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using r′ in capacitance formulas.
- Forgetting ω = 2πf in charging current.
- Thinking Ferranti effect occurs at heavy load.

statements.s: Ferranti effect is prominent on lightly loaded long lines.

quiz.why: The capacitance to neutral of a three-phase line is C = 2πε₀/ln(GMD/r), based on the actual radius r, not the GMR.
In the Ferranti effect, a lightly loaded long line raises the receiving-end voltage. Shunt reactors absorb the line's charging VARs, and so reduce the rise.
Skin effect increases with frequency (and conductor size), since current is pushed to the surface. At DC there is none.
The charging current per phase is I_c = V_ph × ωC, because it is the current into the line capacitance, 90° ahead of voltage.
On a lightly loaded line, the capacitive charging current flowing through the line inductance raises the voltage, so V_R is greater than V_S (Ferranti effect).

questions.q: Unit of load factor
questions.why: Load factor is average load divided by peak load, both in the same unit, so it is a pure ratio with no unit (often shown as a fraction or %).

questions.q: Per-unit Z of a transformer referred to HV vs LV
questions.why: The per-unit impedance of a transformer is the same whichever winding it is referred to, because Z and Z_base scale by the same factor a².

questions.q: Bundled conductors reduce
questions.why: Bundled conductors have a larger effective radius, which lowers the surface electric stress (less corona) and lowers the line inductance.

questions.q: Z_base for 11 kV, 10 MVA
questions.why: Z_base = V²/S = (11)²/10 = 121/10 = 12.1 Ω, using kV and MVA.

questions.q: Diversity factor: Σmax 120 kW, system max 80 kW
questions.why: Diversity factor = (sum of individual maximum demands)/(maximum demand of the system) = 120/80 = 1.5.

questions.q: GMD for spacing 2, 2, 4 m
Assertion (A): Bundled conductors raise the corona inception voltage.  Reason (R): Bundling increases the effective radius, reducing surface electric stress.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Bundling raises the effective radius, which reduces the electric stress at the conductor surface, so corona starts at a higher voltage. R explains A.

questions.q: X = 0.25 pu on 25 MVA, 11 kV → 100 MVA, 11 kV
questions.why: At the same voltage, new pu = old pu × (S_new/S_old) = 0.25 × 100/25 = 1.0 pu.

questions.q: Inductance for equilateral D = 3 m, r = 1.5 cm (per km)
Charging current: 132 kV, C = 1 µF/phase, 50 Hz
Case: A city's 500 MW peak occurs at 8 p.m., but average is 300 MW. Annual energy
questions.why: Annual energy depends on the average load, not the peak: 300 MW × 8760 h = 2 628 000 MWh ≈ 2628 GWh.

questions.q: Motor X = 0.2 pu on 5 MVA, 6.6 kV → 100 MVA, 6.6 kV
questions.why: New pu = 0.2 × 100/5 = 4 pu. Going to a larger base multiplies the pu reactance by the ratio of the bases.

questions.q: 2-conductor bundle GMR with r′ = 1 cm, d = 36 cm
questions.why: For a two-conductor bundle, GMR = √(r′ × d) = √(1 × 36) = 6 cm. The bundle GMR is far bigger than a single conductor's.

questions.q: Capacitance of 3-phase line, GMD 4 m, r = 2 cm (nF/km)
Plant capacity factor: 100 MW plant generating 525.6 GWh/year
questions.why: Capacity factor = actual energy/(rated power × hours) = 525.6 GWh/(100 MW × 8760 h = 876 GWh) = 0.6.

courses.title: Power Systems · Unit 2 · Performance of transmission lines, insulators and cables
courses.summary: Short, medium (nominal-T and nominal-π) and long-line models, ABCD constants, voltage regulation and efficiency, surge impedance and SIL, reactive compensation basics, overhead-line insulators and string efficiency, corona, sag, and underground cables.
outcomes: Model short, medium and long lines with ABCD constants
Compute regulation, efficiency and SIL
Calculate string efficiency and sag
Explain corona and cable insulation stress
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A 33 kV line feeds a factory 20 km away.
Line resistance and reactance cause a voltage drop that depends on load pf.

steps.title: Models
steps.body:
**Short line (< 80 km):** only series Z; A = D = 1, B = Z, C = 0. V_S = V_R + IZ.
Regulation ≈ I(R cos φ_R + X sin φ_R)/V_R (lag).
**Medium (80–250 km):** nominal-π: A = D = 1 + YZ/2, B = Z, C = Y(1 + YZ/4). Nominal-T: A = D = 1 + YZ/2, B = Z(1 + YZ/4), C = Y.
Efficiency = P_R/(P_R + losses).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Short 3-phase line, R = 5 Ω, X = 10 Ω per phase, delivering 10 MW at 33 kV, pf 0.8 lag: I = 10⁷/(√3 × 33 000 × 0.8) = 218.7 A. V_R,ph = 19 053 V.
V_S ≈ 19 053 + 218.7(5 × 0.8 + 10 × 0.6) = 19 053 + 2187 = 21 240 V/ph ⇒ regulation ≈ 11.5%.
Losses = 3 × 218.7² × 5 = 717 kW ⇒ η = 10/10.717 = 93.3%.

**Example 2.** At unity pf (same MW): I = 175 A; drop ≈ 175 × 5 = 875 V ⇒ regulation 4.6%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing line and phase voltages.
- Ignoring that regulation can be negative for leading loads.
- Using short-line approximation for long lines (capacitance matters).

activity.prompt: Short line: V_R = 11 kV/phase-equivalent example — V_S = 12.1 kV, V_R = 11 kV. Regulation (%)?

quiz.why: The ABCD constants of a short line are A = D = 1, B = Z, C = 0. C = 0 since the shunt admittance is ignored.
For a nominal-π line, A = D = 1 + YZ/2, B = Z and C = Y(1 + YZ/4).
By convention, a line up to about 80 km is a short line, where capacitance can be neglected. Up to about 250 km is medium.
Voltage drop ≈ I(R cosφ + X sinφ) for lagging pf, so the reactive term adds. Lagging loads cause a larger drop than unity-pf loads.
For a passive reciprocal two-port, the determinant of ABCD is 1: AD − BC = 1.

lessons.title: Long lines, surge impedance and SIL

scenes.text: Very long AC lines behave like distributed networks with travelling waves.
Surge impedance loading tells the 'natural' power where the line is self-balanced in VARs.

steps.title: Long-line equations
steps.body:
Propagation constant γ = √(zy) = α + jβ; characteristic (surge) impedance Z_c = √(z/y).
A = D = cosh γl, B = Z_c sinh γl, C = sinh(γl)/Z_c.
Lossless: Z_c = √(L/C) (≈ 400 Ω for single-conductor overhead lines, ≈ 250–300 Ω bundled, ≈ 40–60 Ω cables); β = ω√(LC); wavelength ≈ 6000 km at 50 Hz.
**SIL** = V_L²/Z_c — at this load reactive generated by C equals absorbed by L; flat voltage profile.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 400 kV line, Z_c = 250 Ω: SIL = 400²/250 = 640 MW.

**Example 2.** L = 1 mH/km, C = 11 nF/km: Z_c = √(10⁻³/1.1×10⁻⁸) = 301.5 Ω; v = 1/√(LC) = 3.0×10⁵ km/s.

**Example 3.** Lossless 300 km line at no load: V_R = V_S/cos βl, βl = 2π·300/6000 = 0.314 rad ⇒ V_R = 1.051 V_S.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using phase voltage in SIL (use line voltage with 3-phase MW).
- Treating Z_c as a resistance that dissipates power.
- Forgetting cosh/sinh of complex arguments for lossy lines.

activity.prompt: 765 kV line with Z_c = 260 Ω. SIL (MW, ≈)?

quiz.why: The surge impedance of a lossless line is Z_c = √(L/C), set by the inductance and capacitance per unit length.
Surge impedance loading is SIL = V_L²/Z_c (with V_L the line voltage). It is the power delivered into a load equal to Z_c.

quiz.q: At SIL the voltage profile is
quiz.why: At SIL, the reactive power absorbed by the line inductance equals that supplied by the line capacitance, so the voltage profile is flat.
Overhead lines have a surge impedance of roughly 300–400 Ω, so about 400 Ω is typical. Cables have much lower values.
For a long line, A = D = cosh(γl), B = Z_c sinh(γl) and C = sinh(γl)/Z_c.

scenes.text: A 132 kV tower hangs strings of 9 or so porcelain discs.
Voltage across the discs is unequal — the one next to the conductor is stressed most.

steps.title: String efficiency
steps.body:
Self-capacitance C of each disc and shunt (disc-to-tower) capacitance mC cause unequal distribution.
For 3 discs (top to bottom V₁, V₂, V₃): V₂ = V₁(1 + m), V₃ = V₁(1 + 3m + m²).
String efficiency = V_total/(n × V_max) × 100.
Improvement: longer cross-arms (smaller m), grading discs (capacitance grading), guard (grading) ring.

steps.title: Corona and sag
steps.body:
Corona: ionisation of air around conductors when surface gradient exceeds ~30 kV/cm (peak) at NTP — hissing, violet glow, power loss, radio interference, ozone. Critical disruptive voltage V_d = m₀ g₀ δ r ln(D/r) (g₀ ≈ 21.1 kV_rms/cm). Reduced by larger diameter or bundling.
Sag (supports at equal level): S = wl²/(8T) for span l, weight w per unit length, tension T (wind and ice add to w vectorially).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming equal voltage across all discs.
- Using tension in kN with w in N/m inconsistently.
- Forgetting that corona loss rises in rain and fog.

activity.prompt: Sag: span 250 m, w = 8 N/m, T = 25 kN. Sag (m)?

quiz.why: In a string of insulators, the disc closest to the conductor has the maximum voltage, since it carries the charging current for all the discs' shunt capacitances.
A guard ring around the lowest disc equalises the voltage distribution along the string, improving string efficiency.
Corona starts when the surface electric stress is high. A larger conductor diameter or bundling lowers the stress, so corona is reduced.
For a span with level supports, the sag (parabolic approximation) is S = wl²/(8T), with w weight per unit length, l span, T tension.
String efficiency = (voltage across the string)/(n × voltage across the worst disc). 100% means every disc takes the same voltage.

scenes.text: Dense cities bury 66–220 kV cables to avoid overhead lines.
Cables have high capacitance — useful to know when energising them.

steps.title: Cables
steps.body: Single-core cable: conductor radius r, sheath radius R. Insulation resistance R_ins = (ρ/2πl) ln(R/r). Capacitance C = 2πε₀εᵣ l/ln(R/r). Maximum stress at the conductor surface: g_max = V/(r ln(R/r)); minimum at the sheath. Most economical: r = R/e (ln(R/r) = 1) ⇒ g_max = V/r. Grading (capacitance or intersheath) equalises stress. XLPE has replaced paper-oil in most new cables.

steps.title: Reactive compensation
steps.body: Shunt capacitors: raise voltage, supply VARs under heavy load. Shunt reactors: absorb VARs at light load (Ferranti). Series capacitors: reduce line reactance, raise power transfer and stability. SVC/STATCOM: fast controllable VARs.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 66 kV three-phase cable (phase voltage 38.1 kV rms), r = 1 cm, R = 2.5 cm: g_max = 38.1/(1 × ln 2.5) = 41.6 kV/cm rms.

**Example 2.** Capacitance per km with εᵣ = 3.5: C = 2π × 8.854×10⁻¹² × 3.5 × 1000/0.916 = 0.212 µF/km.

**Example 3.** Series compensation 40% of X = 100 Ω ⇒ X_eff = 60 Ω ⇒ P_max increases by 1/0.6 = 1.67×.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using line instead of phase voltage for cable stress (stress is to earth/sheath).
- Forgetting that cable charging current limits long AC cable lengths (HVDC used for long sea links).
- Placing series capacitors without protection against overvoltage during faults.

activity.prompt: Device → effect

quiz.q: Max dielectric stress in a cable occurs at
quiz.why: In a single-core cable, the field is g = V/(x ln(R/r)), so it is highest at the smallest x, i.e. at the conductor surface.
For the lowest g_max for a given V and R, the optimum is ln(R/r) = 1, so r = R/e. That is the most economical conductor radius.
Series capacitors cancel part of the line reactance, so X falls and the transfer limit P = EV sinδ/X rises. This increases power transfer capability.
Long undersea AC cables have a huge charging current, which uses up the capacity. HVDC has no charging current, so it is used for long sea links.
Cable capacitance per length is C = 2πε₀ε_r/ln(R/r), so it is proportional to ε_r/ln(R/r).

questions.q: Short line is modelled by
questions.why: A short line has negligible shunt capacitance, so it is modelled by its series impedance (R + jX) only.

questions.q: Shunt reactors are used at
questions.why: Shunt reactors are used at light load, when the line's charging current causes a voltage rise (Ferranti). The reactor absorbs the extra VARs.

questions.q: Disc nearest to conductor has
questions.why: The disc nearest to the conductor carries the highest voltage in a string. The disc nearest the cross-arm carries the least.

questions.q: Regulation: V_S 35 kV, V_R 33 kV
SIL of 220 kV line with Z_c = 400 Ω
Sag for span 200 m, w = 6 N/m, T = 12 kN
Assertion (A): Receiving-end voltage can exceed sending-end voltage at light load.  Reason (R): Charging current flowing through series inductance raises voltage along the line.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. At light load, capacitive charging current flows through the line inductance and raises the voltage along the line, so V_R can exceed V_S. R explains A.

questions.q: 3-disc string, m = 0.2, V₁ = 10 kV: V₃
questions.why: V₂ = V₁(1 + m) = 12 kV and V₃ = V₁(1 + 3m + m²) = 10(1 + 0.6 + 0.04) = 16.4 kV. The discs nearer the line take more voltage.

questions.q: String efficiency for that case
questions.why: String efficiency = (10 + 12 + 16.4)/(3 × 16.4) = 38.4/49.2 ≈ 78%. It is below 100% since the voltage is not shared equally.

questions.q: Lossless line no-load V_R/V_S for βl = 0.4 rad
questions.why: For a lossless line at no load, V_S = V_R cos βl, so V_R/V_S = 1/cos 0.4 = 1/0.921 ≈ 1.086. It shows the Ferranti rise.

questions.q: Case: A 33 kV short line (R 4, X 8 Ω/phase) supplies 6 MW at 0.8 lag. Approx. voltage drop per phase
Line losses for that case
questions.why: Three-phase line loss = 3I²R = 3 × 131² × 4 ≈ 206 000 W ≈ 206 kW.

questions.q: Cable g_max: V = 33 kV (to sheath), r = 1 cm, R = e cm
questions.why: g_max = V/(r ln(R/r)). With R = e·r, ln(R/r) = 1, so g_max = 33 kV/(1 cm × 1) = 33 kV/cm.

courses.title: Power Systems · Unit 3 · Fault analysis and symmetrical components
courses.summary: Symmetrical three-phase faults with per-unit reactance diagrams, short-circuit MVA and current-limiting reactors, symmetrical components and sequence networks, and unsymmetrical faults: single line-to-ground, line-to-line and double line-to-ground.
outcomes: Compute symmetrical fault currents and fault MVA
Size current-limiting reactors
Transform phasors into sequence components
Analyse LG, LL and LLG faults with sequence networks
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A substation needs breakers that can interrupt the worst short circuit.
A three-phase fault calculation in per-unit gives that current.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Draw the per-unit reactance diagram on a common base; Thevenin at the fault point: V_f (usually 1 pu prefault) and X_th. Fault current I_f = V_f/X_th pu; actual I = I_f × I_base.
Short-circuit MVA = S_base/X_th(pu) (for V_f = 1).
Generator reactances: subtransient X″_d (first cycles), transient X′_d, synchronous X_d (steady state).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Generator 50 MVA, 11 kV, X″ = 0.2 pu, feeding through a transformer 50 MVA, X = 0.1 pu; fault at HV (132 kV). X_th = 0.3 pu (50 MVA base) ⇒ I_f = 3.33 pu; I_base(132 kV) = 50e6/(√3·132e3) = 218.7 A ⇒ I_f = 729 A; fault MVA = 50/0.3 = 167 MVA.

**Example 2.** Two identical generator–transformer units (0.3 pu each) in parallel feeding the HV bus: X_th = 0.3 ∥ 0.3 = 0.15 pu ⇒ fault MVA = 50/0.15 = 333 MVA — the fault level doubles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a base current from the wrong voltage zone.
- Mixing subtransient and transient reactances.
- Forgetting that adding parallel sources increases fault level.

activity.prompt: Fault MVA if X_th = 0.25 pu on a 100 MVA base?

quiz.why: Fault MVA = S_base/X_th (in pu) with 1 pu prefault voltage, since the fault current in pu is 1/X_th.

quiz.q: Reactance used for breaker interrupting (first cycles)
quiz.why: For breaker interrupting duty in the first cycles, the subtransient reactance X″_d is used, because it gives the highest current right after the fault.

quiz.q: Adding generators in parallel makes fault level
quiz.why: Adding generators in parallel lowers the Thevenin reactance X_th at the bus, so fault current and fault level go up.
The prefault voltage is normally taken as 1.0 pu, which simplifies calculation. Loads are usually neglected.
I_f = V/X = 1/0.2 = 5 pu. Smaller reactance gives larger fault current.

story.title: When the grid gets too strong

scenes.text: As a city grid grows, fault levels exceed old breakers' ratings.
Series reactors limit fault current without replacing every breaker.

steps.title: Placement
steps.body: Generator reactors (in series with each generator), feeder reactors (each feeder), bus-bar (tie) reactors between sections, ring systems. Reactors have low resistance (to limit losses) and are air-cored (linear at high currents).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Bus fault level 500 MVA (100 MVA base ⇒ X_th = 0.2 pu); breakers rated 300 MVA ⇒ required X_total = 100/300 = 0.333 ⇒ add 0.133 pu reactor (per-unit on 100 MVA). At 11 kV: Z_base = 1.21 Ω ⇒ X = 0.161 Ω.

**Example 2.** % reactance of a reactor: X% = (I_rated X/V_ph) × 100. A 1000 A, 11 kV reactor with X = 0.254 Ω: X% = 1000 × 0.254/6351 × 100 = 4%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using an iron-cored reactor (saturates at fault current).
- Placing reactors where they cause large normal voltage drops.
- Converting percentage reactance with the wrong base.

activity.prompt: Bus X_th = 0.25 pu (100 MVA base); breaker limit 250 MVA. Additional reactor needed (pu)?

quiz.why: Current-limiting reactors are air-cored, so they do not saturate. Their reactance stays linear even at the high fault current.
The main purpose of a reactor is to limit fault current, so that breakers and equipment are not overstressed.
Bus-section reactors connect sections of a busbar and limit the fault current each section sees from the others.
Feeder reactors carry normal load current too, which causes a continuous voltage drop and I²R-type losses. That is their drawback.

quiz.q: Required X_total for 400 MVA limit on 100 MVA base
quiz.why: Fault MVA = S_base/X. So X = 100/400 = 0.25 pu is the total reactance needed to limit the fault to 400 MVA.

scenes.text: An unbalanced set of three phasors looks messy.
It is exactly the sum of three balanced sets: positive, negative and zero sequence.

steps.title: Transformation
steps.body:
a = 1∠120°. V_a = V₀ + V₁ + V₂; V_b = V₀ + a²V₁ + aV₂; V_c = V₀ + aV₁ + a²V₂.
Inverse: V₀ = (V_a + V_b + V_c)/3; V₁ = (V_a + aV_b + a²V_c)/3; V₂ = (V_a + a²V_b + aV_c)/3.
Zero-sequence currents need a neutral/earth return: I_n = 3I₀.

steps.title: Sequence networks
steps.body:
Generators produce only positive-sequence EMF. Positive and negative impedances of static equipment (lines, transformers) are equal; for rotating machines Z₂ < Z₁ typically.
Zero-sequence: depends on earthing and transformer connections — Y-grounded passes zero sequence; Δ blocks it from the line but circulates internally; neutral impedance Z_n appears as 3Z_n.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** I_a = 10∠0°, I_b = 0, I_c = 0: I₀ = I₁ = I₂ = 3.33∠0° A.

**Example 2.** Balanced set V_a = 1∠0°, V_b = 1∠−120°, V_c = 1∠120°: V₁ = 1, V₂ = V₀ = 0.

**Example 3.** Neutral current with I₀ = 5 A: I_n = 15 A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Order of a and a² in the transformation.
- Forgetting 3Z_n in zero-sequence networks.
- Assuming Δ windings pass zero-sequence current to the line.

activity.prompt: Sequence fact

quiz.why: The zero-sequence component is the average of the three phase voltages: V₀ = (V_a + V_b + V_c)/3. The other sequences use the operator a.
The operator a = 1∠120°. The three vectors 1, a and a² are equally spaced, so they add to zero: 1 + a + a² = 0.
A balanced three-phase system contains only the positive-sequence component. Negative and zero sequences appear only in unbalance.
Zero-sequence currents are equal in all phases, so they need a return path through the neutral or earth to flow.
I₁ = (I_a + aI_b + a²I_c)/3 = 9/3 = 3 A. With only one phase current, each sequence component is one-third of it.

scenes.text: A tree branch touching one line causes a single line-to-ground fault.
About 70–80% of overhead-line faults are LG faults.

steps.title: Sequence connections at the fault (prefault E = 1 pu)
steps.body:
- **LG (phase a):** sequence networks in series: I₁ = I₂ = I₀ = E/(Z₁ + Z₂ + Z₀ + 3Z_f); I_f = 3I₀.
- **LL (b–c):** positive and negative in parallel (opposed), no zero: I₁ = −I₂ = E/(Z₁ + Z₂ + Z_f); I_f = √3|I₁|.
- **LLG (b–c–g):** positive in series with (negative ∥ (zero + 3Z_f)): I₁ = E/(Z₁ + Z₂∥(Z₀ + 3Z_f)).
Severity usually: 3-phase > LLG > LL > LG (but LG can exceed 3-phase if Z₀ is small).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting 3Z_f (or 3Z_n) in the zero-sequence branch.
- Using I_f = I₀ for LG (it is 3I₀).
- Including the zero-sequence network in an LL fault.

activity.prompt: LG fault: Z₁ = j0.25, Z₂ = j0.25, Z₀ = j0.1 pu, solid. Fault current magnitude (pu)?

quiz.q: LG fault: sequence networks are connected in
quiz.why: For a line-to-ground fault, the boundary conditions require I₀ = I₁ = I₂, so the three sequence networks are connected in series.
A line-to-line fault has no connection to ground, so there is no zero-sequence current. The zero-sequence network is excluded.
In an LG fault, I₀ = I₁ = I₂ and I_a = I₀ + I₁ + I₂ = 3I₀. So the fault current is three times the zero-sequence current.

quiz.q: Most frequent fault on overhead lines
quiz.why: Single line-to-ground faults are the most common on overhead lines (about 70–80%), often caused by lightning or contact with trees. Three-phase faults are rare.
In an LL fault, I₀ = 0 and I₂ = −I₁, so I_b = (a² − a)I₁ = −j√3 I₁. The magnitude is √3|I₁|.

Zero-sequence components are
questions.why: Zero-sequence components are equal in magnitude and in phase in all three phases, so there is no 120° displacement.
options: equal in magnitude and phase in all three phases

questions.q: Current-limiting reactors are
questions.why: Current-limiting reactors are air-cored so that they do not saturate under the heavy fault current, keeping their reactance linear.

questions.q: I_base at 33 kV, 100 MVA
Fault MVA for X_th = 0.4 pu, 50 MVA base
questions.why: Fault MVA = S_base/X_th = 50/0.4 = 125 MVA.

questions.q: I_n for I₀ = 2 kA
questions.why: The neutral current is I_n = 3I₀ = 3 × 2 = 6 kA, because the three equal zero-sequence phase currents add in the neutral.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A delta–star transformer (star grounded) passes no zero-sequence current from the delta side line.  Reason (R): Zero-sequence currents circulate inside the delta and cannot leave through its line terminals.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. In a delta winding, zero-sequence currents can circulate inside the delta, but they cannot flow out through the line terminals because they are in phase with each other. So R explains A.

LG fault with Z_f = j0.1, Z₁ = Z₂ = j0.2, Z₀ = j0.1
questions.why: For an LG fault, I_f = 3E/(Z₀ + Z₁ + Z₂ + 3Z_f) = 3/(0.1 + 0.2 + 0.2 + 0.3) = 3/0.8 = 3.75 pu. The fault impedance counts three times in the series loop.

questions.why: At 600 MVA the bus X = 100/600 = 0.1667 pu; for 400 MVA it must be 100/400 = 0.25 pu. The reactor needed is 0.25 − 0.1667 ≈ 0.083 pu.

scenes.text: Grid control centres run load-flow studies every few minutes.
Everything starts from the bus admittance matrix.

steps.title: Y-bus
steps.body:
Y_ii = sum of admittances connected to bus i (including line charging/2); Y_ij = −(admittance between i and j). Symmetric (no phase shifters) and sparse.
Bus types: **slack/swing** (V, δ specified — balances losses), **PV/generator** (P, |V| specified), **PQ/load** (P, Q specified).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Three buses, lines 1–2: y = −j10, 1–3: −j5, 2–3: −j4 (pu): Y₁₁ = −j15, Y₂₂ = −j14, Y₃₃ = −j9; Y₁₂ = j10, Y₁₃ = j5, Y₂₃ = j4.

**Example 2.** Add line charging B/2 = j0.1 at each end of line 1–2: Y₁₁ = −j14.9, Y₂₂ = −j13.9.

steps.title: Power-flow equations
steps.body: P_i − jQ_i = V_i* Σ Y_ik V_k. Non-linear ⇒ iterative solution. Unknowns: PQ bus |V|, δ; PV bus δ (Q computed, with limits); slack P, Q.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Positive sign for off-diagonal elements (they are negative of line admittance).
- Forgetting shunt (charging) admittances on the diagonal.
- Treating the slack bus voltage as unknown.

activity.prompt: Bus type

quiz.why: In the Y-bus, the off-diagonal term is the negative of the admittance between buses i and j: Y_ij = −y_ij. The diagonal is the sum of connected admittances.
A power system Y-bus is sparse, since most buses connect to only a few others, and symmetric when there are no phase shifters.
At a PV (generator) bus, the real power P and the voltage magnitude |V| are specified, while Q and δ are found.
The slack bus has fixed voltage and angle and supplies whatever real and reactive power is needed to balance the load plus the losses, which are not known beforehand.

quiz.q: Y₁₁ with lines −j10 and −j5 to bus 1
quiz.why: The diagonal Y₁₁ is the sum of the admittances connected to bus 1: −j10 + (−j5) = −j15.

scenes.text: A national grid model has tens of thousands of buses.
Newton–Raphson converges in a handful of iterations — the industry standard.

steps.title: Gauss–Seidel
steps.body: V_i^(k+1) = (1/Y_ii)[(P_i − jQ_i)/V_i*^(k) − Σ_(j<i) Y_ij V_j^(k+1) − Σ_(j>i) Y_ij V_j^(k)]. Simple, low memory; slow linear convergence (iterations grow with system size); acceleration factor ≈ 1.6 helps.

steps.title: Newton–Raphson
steps.body: Solve [ΔP; ΔQ] = J [Δδ; Δ|V|] each iteration (J = Jacobian of ∂P/∂δ, ∂P/∂V, ∂Q/∂δ, ∂Q/∂V). Quadratic convergence (3–5 iterations), more computation per iteration. **Fast decoupled** load flow: neglects weak couplings (P–V, Q–δ) and uses constant matrices — very fast for transmission systems.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (one GS step).** Two-bus: slack V₁ = 1∠0, load bus 2 with S₂ = −(0.5 + j0.2) pu (load), line y = −j10 ⇒ Y₂₂ = −j10, Y₂₁ = j10. Start V₂ = 1∠0:
V₂ = (1/−j10)[(−0.5 + j0.2)/1 − j10(1)] = (1/−j10)(−0.5 − j9.8) = 0.98 − j0.05 ⇒ |V₂| ≈ 0.981, δ ≈ −2.9°.

**Example 2.** Number of NR equations for a system with 1 slack, 4 PV, 10 PQ buses: P equations 14 + Q equations 10 = 24.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Updating PV bus voltage magnitude (keep |V| fixed, adjust angle).
- Forgetting Q limits at PV buses (convert to PQ if violated).
- Sign of load power (injection negative).

activity.prompt: NR load-flow equations count: 1 slack, 3 PV, 8 PQ buses (P eqs + Q eqs)?

quiz.why: Newton–Raphson uses a Jacobian to linearise the equations at each step, and near the solution the error is roughly squared each iteration. This quadratic convergence means it needs few iterations.
Gauss–Seidel is simple, needs little memory and is easy to program, so it suits small systems or a rough first solution. For large systems it is slow, as it converges only linearly.

quiz.q: Fast decoupled method neglects coupling between
quiz.why: The fast decoupled method assumes P is mainly tied to the angle δ and Q to the voltage magnitude |V|. So it neglects the weak P–V and Q–δ couplings, making the Jacobian constant and faster to use.

quiz.q: At a PV bus, which is updated?
quiz.why: At a PV bus, |V| is fixed by the generator and P is specified, so only the angle is updated. Q is then computed from the result, and checked against limits.
An acceleration factor of about 1.6 is typical in Gauss–Seidel load flow. It over-corrects each step slightly and so speeds up convergence. Values near 2 or above can make it diverge.

scenes.text: A fault that isn't cleared fast enough can make generators lose synchronism.
The critical clearing time is the deadline for protection.

steps.title: Swing equation
steps.body:
(2H/ω_s) d²δ/dt² = P_m − P_e (pu), H = stored KE at synchronous speed/MVA rating (MJ/MVA), typically 2–9 s. P_e = P_max sin δ.
M = H/(πf) pu·s²/electrical radian (for 50 Hz).

steps.title: Equal-area criterion (single machine–infinite bus)
steps.body:
Stable if the accelerating area A₁ (P_m > P_e, during fault) can be balanced by a decelerating area A₂ (P_e > P_m, after clearing) before δ reaches δ_max = π − δ₀′.
For a 3-phase fault at the generator terminals (P_e = 0 during fault), clearing angle cos δ_cr = (π − 2δ₀)sin δ₀ − cos δ₀ (P_m = P_max sin δ₀, same post-fault curve). Critical clearing time t_cr = √(4H(δ_cr − δ₀)/(ω_s P_m)).
Steady-state limit: P < P_max; transient stability improved by fast breakers, higher voltage, series capacitors, autoreclosing, fast valving.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing degrees and radians in δ_cr and t_cr.
- Using the MVA of the system instead of the machine for H.
- Thinking equal-area works directly for multi-machine systems (needs numerical integration).

activity.prompt: Generator 200 MVA with H = 4 MJ/MVA. Stored kinetic energy (MJ)?

quiz.why: The inertia constant H = (kinetic energy at rated speed)/(MVA rating), so its unit is MJ/MVA, which equals seconds.

The equal-area criterion says the system stays stable if the kinetic energy gained during the fault (accelerating area) can be given back after clearing (decelerating area). It compares those two areas on the P–δ curve.
A faster clearing time gives the rotor less time to accelerate, so the accelerating area A₁ is smaller. It then needs a smaller decelerating area, improving transient stability.
The steady-state limit comes from P = (EV/X) sinδ, which is a maximum at δ = 90°, giving P_max = EV/X. Beyond that, extra mechanical input cannot be matched.
Series capacitors cancel part of the line reactance. Since P_max = EV/X, a lower X raises P_max and gives a bigger stability margin.

lessons.title: Protection: relays, circuit breakers and earthing

scenes.text: When a fault hits one feeder, only that feeder trips — the rest of the city stays lit.
That is selective protection: relays, CTs/PTs and breakers.

steps.title: Relays and schemes
steps.body:
Requirements: selectivity, speed, sensitivity, reliability, stability.
- **Overcurrent:** IDMT (inverse definite minimum time) characteristics; time-graded for radial feeders. Plug setting multiplier PSM = fault current/(pickup × CT ratio).
- **Directional overcurrent** for ring mains.
- **Distance (impedance/mho):** measures V/I ⇒ zones 1 (≈ 80% line, instantaneous), 2 (≈ 120%, delayed), 3 (backup).
- **Differential (Merz-Price):** compares currents in/out — transformers, generators, bus bars (percentage-bias against CT mismatch).
- Buchholz relay for oil transformer internal faults.

steps.title: Breakers and earthing
steps.body:
Circuit breakers interrupt fault current at current zero: air-blast, SF₆ (EHV), vacuum (MV, up to 33 kV); minimum oil (older). Ratings: breaking (symmetrical/asymmetrical) and making current (≈ 2.55 × rms symmetrical breaking). Fuses and MCBs for LV.
Neutral earthing: solid, resistance, reactance, Petersen coil (arc suppression, tuned to line capacitance: X_L = 1/(3ωC)).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Relay set at 125% of 5 A CT secondary (pickup 6.25 A), CT 400/5, fault 4000 A: secondary = 50 A ⇒ PSM = 8. With TMS 0.2 and IDMT (3 s at PSM 10 standard curve ≈ 3.2 s at 8): t ≈ 0.2 × 3.2 = 0.64 s.

**Example 2.** Breaker symmetrical breaking 20 kA ⇒ making ≈ 2.55 × 20 = 51 kA peak.

**Example 3.** Petersen coil for C = 1 µF/phase at 50 Hz: L = 1/(3ω²C) = 1/(3 × 98 696 × 10⁻⁶) = 3.38 H.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Grading relays so the upstream relay trips first (lose selectivity).
- Ignoring CT saturation in differential schemes.
- Using vacuum breakers above their typical voltage class.

activity.prompt: Protection task → typical relay/device

quiz.why: Zone 1 is set to cover about 80% of the protected line and trip instantly. The margin avoids overreach caused by errors in measurement and line data, which could trip for faults on the next line.
Differential protection compares the current entering with that leaving a protected zone, using Kirchhoff's current law. A difference means a fault inside the zone, and it trips.
The making current is the peak (asymmetric) current a breaker must close onto, about 2.55 times the symmetrical breaking current (rms). The factor includes the DC offset.
Vacuum breakers are widely used in medium voltage, since they are compact and need little maintenance. The vacuum quickly quenches the arc.

quiz.q: PSM for 30 A secondary, pickup 5 A
quiz.why: Plug setting multiplier = fault current in the relay/pickup current = 30/5 = 6. It tells how many times the pickup the relay sees.

questions.q: Slack bus specifies
questions.why: The slack (swing) bus has a specified voltage magnitude and angle, V and δ. Its P and Q follow from the solution, as it balances the system.

questions.q: NR method uses
questions.why: Newton–Raphson load flow linearises the power equations using the Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives, and solves for corrections at each iteration.

questions.q: Breaker medium for EHV
questions.why: For EHV (extra-high voltage) systems, SF₆ gas breakers are common because the gas has excellent arc-quenching and insulating properties. Water cannot be used and air blast is used only for a few designs.

questions.q: Y₂₂ for lines −j8 (1–2) and −j4 (2–3)
questions.why: The diagonal element Y₂₂ is the sum of admittances connected to bus 2: −j8 + (−j4) = −j12.

questions.q: KE stored: 500 MVA, H = 3
questions.why: Kinetic energy = H × S = 3 MJ/MVA × 500 MVA = 1500 MJ. H is the stored energy per MVA of rating.

questions.q: Zone 2 of a distance relay is
questions.why: Zone 2 of a distance relay reaches beyond the end of the protected line (about 120% or more), but with a time delay. It gives backup for the remote end and for zone 1 failure.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Newton–Raphson load flow converges in fewer iterations than Gauss–Seidel.  Reason (R): NR has quadratic convergence using the Jacobian.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Newton–Raphson uses the Jacobian, and its convergence is quadratic, so it needs far fewer iterations than Gauss–Seidel, which is only linear. R explains A.

questions.q: δ₀ for P_m = 0.707 P_max
questions.why: Mechanical input P_m = P_max sinδ₀, so sinδ₀ = 0.707 and δ₀ = sin⁻¹(0.707) = 45°.

questions.q: Petersen coil L for C = 2 µF/phase, 50 Hz
questions.why: A Petersen coil resonates with the line capacitance to ground: 3ωC·ωL = 1, so L = 1/(3ω²C) = 1/(3 × 98 696 × 2×10⁻⁶) ≈ 1.69 H. It cancels the capacitive earth-fault current.

questions.q: Critical clearing angle for δ₀ = 30° (3-phase fault at terminals, same pre/post curve)
questions.why: With the same pre-fault and post-fault curve and zero power during the fault, cosδ_cr = (π − 2δ₀) sinδ₀ − cosδ₀ = (3.1416 − 1.0472)(0.5) − 0.866 ≈ 0.181. So δ_cr ≈ 79.6°.

questions.q: Case: An IDMT relay with CT 200/1 and pickup 1 A sees a 2000 A fault. PSM
questions.why: Secondary fault current = 2000 A/(200/1) = 10 A. PSM = 10 A/1 A pickup = 10.

questions.q: NR equations: 1 slack, 2 PV, 5 PQ
questions.why: With 1 slack, 2 PV and 5 PQ buses (8 in all), NR needs P equations for the 7 non-slack buses and Q equations for the 5 PQ buses: 7 + 5 = 12.

questions.q: GS one step for V₂ (slack 1∠0, y = −j5, S₂ = −0.2 pu real only, V₂⁰ = 1)
questions.why: Gauss–Seidel: V₂ = (1/Y₂₂)[(P − jQ)/V₂* − Y₂₁V₁]. With Y₂₂ = −j5, Y₂₁ = +j5, P − jQ = −0.2: V₂ = (1/−j5)(−0.2 − j5) = 1 − j0.04.

questions.q: t_cr for H = 4, f = 50, P_m = 1 pu, δ_cr − δ₀ = 0.8 rad
questions.why: Critical clearing time t_cr = √(4H(δ_cr − δ₀)/(ω_s P_m)) = √(4 × 4 × 0.8/314.16) = √0.0407 ≈ 0.20 s.

questions.q: Making current rating for 40 kA breaking
questions.why: Making current ≈ 2.55 × breaking current = 2.55 × 40 kA ≈ 102 kA. The breaker must be able to close onto a fault, with its DC offset.

questions.q: Base-load plants

questions.why: A Petersen coil (arc-suppression coil) is connected from neutral to earth. It cancels the capacitive earth-fault current, so arcing earth faults extinguish themselves.
